Most arrests happen within minutes of induction and many are pulseless electrical activity or bradycardia.

Four mechanisms combine. Hypoxaemia from apnoea in a patient with poor reserve. Hypotension from loss of sympathetic tone with induction and reduced venous return from positive pressure. Worsening acidosis when a compensating patient becomes apnoeic and is then under-ventilated. And right-ventricular failure when hypoxia, hypercapnia and positive pressure raise pulmonary vascular resistance in a ventricle already at its limit.
Hypoxaemia: optimise pre-oxygenation with NIV or a PEEP valve, use apnoeic oxygenation, ventilate gently during apnoea if needed, and aim for first-pass success.

Hypotension: treat volume depletion with fluid or blood, start or increase a vasopressor infusion before induction (many teams target a systolic pressure above about 90–100 or MAP above 65 before proceeding), have push-dose vasopressors ready, and reduce the induction dose. Avoid propofol in shock.

Acidosis: minimise apnoea time; immediately after intubation set a minute ventilation matching the pre-intubation effort. Some clinicians consider bicarbonate in extreme acidaemia as a bridge, though evidence is limited.

RV failure: avoid hypotension and hypoxia; consider an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator if available; use modest PEEP and tidal volumes; consider awake or delayed approaches and the smallest possible induction dose.

Check pressure every one to three minutes after induction. If it falls: give a push-dose vasopressor, increase the infusion, reduce PEEP and tidal volume temporarily if positive pressure is limiting venous return, rule out tension pneumothorax and auto-PEEP by disconnecting briefly, and treat bleeding.

If the patient arrests, start high-quality CPR and follow ACLS, and look for reversible causes particular to this setting: hypoxia (tube position, DOPE), hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, acidosis, hyperkalaemia (succinylcholine in a susceptible patient), and auto-PEEP. Disconnecting the ventilator for 30–60 seconds treats breath stacking.

A 55-year-old after hip surgery with sudden dyspnoea: SpO₂ 84 % on a non-rebreather, BP 86/52, HR 128, distended neck veins, RV dilation on bedside ultrasound. He is tiring and the team considers intubation before transfer to a centre for catheter-directed therapy.

This patient is at extreme risk of arrest at induction: a failing, pressure-loaded right ventricle that depends on sympathetic tone and preload, combined with hypoxaemia. Positive pressure raises RV afterload and reduces venous return.

A tracheostomy is an opening into the trachea; the upper airway is still connected to the lungs. These patients can, in principle, be oxygenated from the mouth and nose, or intubated orally, once the stoma is covered.

A laryngectomy removes the larynx and brings the trachea out as an end stoma; there is no connection between the mouth and the lungs. Oxygen must go to the stoma. Oral intubation is impossible. Bedside signs, wristbands and the patient's own information should make clear which type you are dealing with.

Call for help, apply oxygen to both the face and the stoma, and assess patency. Remove any speaking valve or cap, remove the inner cannula if present (many blockages are in the inner tube), and pass a suction catheter. If the catheter passes easily, the tube is likely patent: continue assessment and ventilate.

If the catheter will not pass, deflate the cuff and reassess. If the patient is still not breathing adequately, remove the tracheostomy tube. Then oxygenate: for a tracheostomy, by standard upper-airway methods with the stoma covered, or via the stoma with a paediatric face mask or a laryngeal mask applied to the stoma; for a laryngectomy, via the stoma only.

Secondary steps: oral intubation (tracheostomy patients only) or intubation of the stoma with a smaller tracheostomy or endotracheal tube, ideally over a bougie or with a fibreoptic scope. A new or fresh tracheostomy (less than about 7 days) has an immature tract that may close or allow a false passage, so recannulation is riskier.

Angioedema: from ACE inhibitors (bradykinin-mediated, does not respond reliably to adrenaline or antihistamines), hereditary angioedema, or anaphylaxis (histamine-mediated, responds to IM adrenaline). Look for voice change, stridor, drooling and tongue or floor-of-mouth swelling. An awake fibreoptic nasal approach by an expert, with a surgical airway prepared, is often preferred when swelling is progressing.

Inhalation injury: soot in the airway, facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarseness or stridor after fire in an enclosed space. Swelling progresses over hours, worsened by resuscitation fluids. Early intubation with a large tube (7.5–8.0 or more for bronchoscopy) before transport is often indicated when signs of airway involvement exist.

Penetrating neck trauma: an expanding haematoma can distort and compress the airway. Avoid blind techniques that may enter a false passage; consider an awake approach or early surgical airway with a surgeon present. Airway injury with air bubbling from the wound may be intubated directly through the wound in extremis.

Obesity: rapid desaturation, difficult mask ventilation and difficult surgical airway. Ramp, head up, pre-oxygenate with PEEP, use apnoeic oxygenation and video laryngoscopy, and mark the membrane by ultrasound if possible.

A 6-year-old with a tracheostomy on home ventilation becomes acutely distressed during transfer: SpO₂ 82 %, no chest rise with the ventilator, high-pressure alarms. Parents say the tube was changed yesterday and the stoma is mature.
The airway is probably blocked or displaced. Parents are a resource — they often know the tube size, how to change it, and the child's baseline.

A sustained, rectangular capnography waveform over several breaths confirms that the tube delivers gas to and from perfused lungs. Professional guidelines treat continuous waveform capnography as mandatory for confirmation and monitoring of every intubated patient, including during transport. "No trace = wrong place" until proven otherwise.

An oesophageal tube may briefly show CO₂ if the stomach contains exhaled gas from mask ventilation or carbonated drinks, but the trace decays to zero within a few breaths. A tube above the cords can show a trace but will leak and dislodge.

In cardiac arrest, CO₂ delivery to the lungs falls with low flow, but high-quality CPR usually produces a measurable, if low, waveform. A flat trace during CPR should prompt reassessment of tube position (visualise with the laryngoscope) rather than acceptance.

Visualising the tube pass through the cords is strong evidence at the time but does not protect against later displacement. Breath sounds are unreliable in noisy aircraft and may be transmitted from the stomach. Chest rise, misting of the tube and colorimetric CO₂ detectors support placement but are less reliable than waveforms. Ultrasound can show tracheal versus oesophageal placement and bilateral lung sliding. A chest X-ray shows depth, not tracheal versus oesophageal placement.

Oesophageal detector devices (bulb or syringe) are unreliable in obesity, pregnancy and with copious secretions. Pulse oximetry falls late after oesophageal intubation, particularly after good pre-oxygenation — saturation can remain high for minutes with the tube in the oesophagus.

In adults, a depth of about 21 cm at the incisors in women and 23 cm in men is typical; in children over about two years, three times the tube size or (age ÷ 2) + 12 cm at the lips. Confirm bilateral air entry and, when available, imaging or ultrasound. Document the depth and recheck it after every move.
Neck flexion moves the tube tip toward the carina; extension moves it toward the cords. In small children a few centimetres of movement can extubate or cause mainstem intubation.

Cuff pressure should be about 20–30 cmH₂O, measured with a manometer. Over-inflation causes tracheal mucosal ischaemia; under-inflation allows aspiration and leak. At altitude in unpressurised cabins, air in the cuff expands; check and adjust.

Keep capnography connected from intubation to handover. A sudden loss of the waveform means displacement, disconnection or obstruction until proven otherwise; a sudden fall to a low value suggests cardiac arrest or massive embolism; a gradual rise suggests hypoventilation or rising metabolism; a "shark-fin" upstroke suggests bronchospasm or obstruction.
Before every move — onto the stretcher, into the aircraft, at the receiving facility — recheck depth and waveform. Many unplanned extubations occur during these transfers.

For children over about two years, the uncuffed tube size is roughly (age ÷ 4) + 4 mm and the cuffed size (age ÷ 4) + 3.5 mm; have a half size above and below ready. Length-based tapes give tube size and drug doses in one step and reduce calculation errors under stress. Depth at the lips is about three times the internal diameter.

Small movements matter: in an infant the trachea may be only 4–5 cm long, so flexion or extension of the head can move the tip from mid-trachea into a main bronchus or out through the cords. Keep the head in a neutral position, tape securely across the upper lip, and recheck depth and capnography after every move and before take-off.
In neonates, the tip-to-lip depth is approximately weight in kilograms + 6 cm. A chest X-ray on arrival confirms the tip sits between the clavicles and the carina.
An intubated patient is moved from the ICU bed to your stretcher, then into the aircraft. On reconnection the waveform is absent and the SpO₂ is still 98 %.

High saturation reassures nobody: a well pre-oxygenated patient can keep a high SpO₂ for minutes after displacement. Loss of the waveform after a move is a displaced or disconnected tube until proven otherwise.

Rigid (Yankauer or large-bore) catheters clear the oropharynx of blood, vomit and particulate matter. Large-bore rigid catheters clear thick material far faster than standard Yankauers. Soft (French) catheters pass through endotracheal and tracheostomy tubes or the nose.

Typical suction pressures are 80–120 mmHg for endotracheal suction in adults (lower in children and neonates, often 60–100 mmHg and 60–80 mmHg respectively); oropharyngeal clearance of heavy contamination may use higher settings. Follow your device and protocol.

Size an endotracheal suction catheter so it occludes no more than about half the internal diameter of the tube; a quick rule is catheter size in French ≈ 2 × the tube size in mm (for example, a 14 Fr catheter for a 7.0 tube). Too large a catheter can evacuate the lungs and cause atelectasis.

Pre-oxygenate with FiO₂ 1.0 for 30–60 seconds. Insert the catheter without suction to the carina or until resistance, withdraw 1 cm, then apply suction while withdrawing with a rotating motion. Limit each pass to about 10–15 seconds in adults (shorter in children). Allow re-oxygenation between passes.

Closed in-line suction systems allow suctioning without disconnecting the ventilator, preserving PEEP and reducing aerosol exposure — preferable in ARDS, high PEEP, and infectious disease. Routine saline instillation is not recommended: it can worsen oxygenation and spread contamination.
Watch for hypoxaemia, bradycardia (vagal stimulation), arrhythmias, raised intracranial pressure, mucosal trauma and bleeding, and bronchospasm.

Massive regurgitation or haemorrhage defeats laryngoscopy and fills the lungs. Position head-up if possible, use a large-bore rigid suction catheter, and lead with it during laryngoscopy (suction-assisted laryngoscopy and airway decontamination, SALAD). After clearing the oropharynx, park the catheter in the upper oesophagus to the left of the blade to control ongoing regurgitation.
After intubation, suction through the tube before ventilating if aspirated material is present; bronchoscopy at the receiving centre may be needed for particulate aspiration.

Check suction at the start of every shift and before every airway: power or battery, canister seated and empty, tubing connected, a rigid catheter and soft catheters of the right sizes, and the vacuum reading with the tubing occluded. Portable units lose strength as batteries drain; a manual hand-powered suction is a useful backup.

Complications are mostly preventable. Hypoxaemia is limited by pre-oxygenation and short passes. Mucosal trauma and bleeding are limited by appropriate pressures, not jabbing the catheter, and stopping 1 cm short of the carina. Atelectasis is limited by catheter size no more than half the tube lumen and by closed systems that preserve PEEP. Infection risk is reduced by sterile technique for endotracheal suction.
Document what you removed — volume, colour, blood or particulate matter — because it informs the receiving team about aspiration, pneumonia or haemorrhage.

Neonates and infants: use lower pressures and smaller catheters, limit each pass to about 5–10 seconds, suction the mouth before the nose (nasal stimulation can trigger a gasp and aspiration of oral contents), and watch for bradycardia. In the newly born, routine deep suction is not recommended; suction only if the airway is obstructed.
Raised intracranial pressure: suctioning causes coughing and surges in ICP. Ensure adequate sedation and analgesia, pre-oxygenate, keep passes short, and avoid repeated passes.
Tracheostomy patients: measure the catheter against the tube length or use pre-measured suction to avoid trauma to the carina. Inner cannulas can be removed and cleaned when secretions are thick.
Infectious disease: closed in-line systems reduce aerosol exposure; wear appropriate PPE for open suction.
An intubated pneumonia patient on a 90-minute flight develops rising peak pressures, a shark-fin capnogram and falling SpO₂. Plateau pressure is unchanged.

A rising peak with an unchanged plateau is a resistance problem; the most likely cause in this patient is secretions in the tube. Dry oxygen and long transport thicken secretions; heat and moisture exchangers help.

Phase I is the inspiratory baseline, near zero, as dead-space gas without CO₂ leaves first. Phase II is the expiratory upstroke as alveolar gas mixes with dead space. Phase III is the alveolar plateau, ending in the end-tidal value (normally 35–45 mmHg). Phase 0 (sometimes called phase IV) is the inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas enters.

EtCO₂ is usually 2–5 mmHg below PaCO₂ in healthy lungs. The gap widens with dead space: low cardiac output, pulmonary embolism, COPD, overdistension, and hypovolaemia. In those patients EtCO₂ underestimates PaCO₂, so trend EtCO₂ against a blood gas.

During CPR, EtCO₂ reflects pulmonary blood flow generated by compressions. A value persistently below about 10 mmHg suggests poor-quality compressions — change compressors, check depth and rate — or a very poor prognosis when it persists after prolonged resuscitation despite good CPR (interpreted alongside other factors, never alone).

A sudden rise in EtCO₂ (often to 35–45 mmHg or more) during compressions is an early sign of return of spontaneous circulation, often before a pulse is palpable. Bicarbonate administration also transiently raises EtCO₂, which must be distinguished from ROSC.
Sedation and opioids: nasal-oral capnography detects hypoventilation and apnoea before oxygen saturation falls, particularly when supplemental oxygen keeps SpO₂ high.
Brain injury: target normocapnia (PaCO₂ 35–40). Establish the PaCO₂–EtCO₂ gap with a blood gas, then ventilate to the EtCO₂ that corresponds; hyperventilate only briefly for signs of herniation.
Metabolic acidosis: in a spontaneously breathing patient a very low EtCO₂ reflects respiratory compensation (for example, in DKA); after intubation, preserving that low CO₂ is essential.
Shock: falling EtCO₂ at constant ventilation suggests falling cardiac output.

End-tidal CO₂ depends on three things: production by metabolism, delivery to the lungs by the circulation, and elimination by ventilation. A change in the number always means one of those three has changed — or the equipment has.
Production rises with fever, shivering, seizures, sepsis, malignant hyperthermia, and when bicarbonate is given (it is converted to CO₂). Production falls with hypothermia and deep sedation.

Delivery depends on cardiac output and pulmonary blood flow. A sudden fall at constant ventilation means falling output, a pulmonary embolism or cardiac arrest; a sudden rise during CPR suggests ROSC.

Elimination depends on alveolar ventilation: rate × (tidal volume − dead space). Hypoventilation raises EtCO₂; hyperventilation lowers it. Increased dead space lowers EtCO₂ relative to PaCO₂ even though the arterial value may be rising.
You transport an intubated septic patient. Over the flight, the capnogram tells a story — if you read it.

CPAP applies one continuous pressure throughout the breath. It recruits collapsed alveoli and increases FRC, reducing shunt and improving oxygenation; in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema it reduces preload and LV afterload by raising intrathoracic pressure; it splints open the upper airway in obstructive sleep apnoea; and it offsets auto-PEEP, reducing the work of triggering in COPD.

BiPAP (bilevel) adds a higher inspiratory pressure (IPAP) above the expiratory pressure (EPAP, equivalent to PEEP). The difference, the pressure support, augments tidal volume and so improves ventilation and CO₂ clearance — the key indication being hypercapnic COPD exacerbation.

Strong evidence supports NIV in acute hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (pH roughly 7.25–7.35) and cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It is also used for pre-oxygenation, in immunocompromised patients with respiratory failure, and in selected asthma and pneumonia patients with close monitoring.

Contraindications: respiratory or cardiac arrest, inability to protect the airway or clear secretions, severely depressed consciousness (except hypercapnic narcosis expected to improve quickly), vomiting or upper GI bleeding, facial trauma or burns preventing a seal, recent upper airway or oesophageal surgery, untreated pneumothorax, and haemodynamic instability (positive pressure lowers venous return).

Reassess within 30–60 minutes and continuously in transport: respiratory rate, work of breathing, SpO₂, EtCO₂ trend, mental status, leak, synchrony and blood pressure. Expected improvement: falling respiratory rate and heart rate, better comfort, improving pH and CO₂.

Failure signs: worsening mental status, inability to tolerate the mask, rising CO₂ or falling pH, persistent tachypnoea, haemodynamic instability, vomiting. Delayed intubation after failed NIV is associated with worse outcomes; in transport, where intubating mid-flight is difficult, the threshold to intubate before departure should be lower if improvement is not clear.
Altitude: mask leak and gastric distension may increase; some transport devices compensate for altitude. Communication is harder under a mask; agree hand signals.

Heated, humidified high-flow nasal oxygen (often 30–60 L/min) delivers a reliable FiO₂, washes CO₂ from the anatomical dead space, produces a small positive pressure, and is comfortable. It is useful in hypoxaemic respiratory failure, for pre-oxygenation and for apnoeic oxygenation. It is oxygen-hungry, which matters for transport oxygen calculations.

The interface decides whether NIV works. Oronasal (full-face) masks suit acute respiratory failure because breathless patients breathe through the mouth. Nasal masks suit calmer patients and allow speech. Total-face masks and helmets spread pressure over a larger area and help when pressure sores or claustrophobia limit other masks.

Fit the mask so it seals without excessive strap tension: one or two fingers should slide under the straps. Small leaks are tolerated by ventilators designed for NIV; large leaks cause asynchrony, failure to trigger or cycle, and dry eyes. Re-fit rather than tighten.

Watch the patient breathe with the machine. Triggering delays, double triggering or breaths that end before the patient finishes inhaling increase work of breathing. Adjust the trigger sensitivity and rise time, coach the patient, and consider low-dose anxiolysis — while never sedating a patient so deeply that airway protection is lost.
Gastric distension, eye irritation, nasal bridge pressure injury and aspiration are the common complications; a gastric tube may be needed on long transports.
A 72-year-old with hypertension is sitting bolt upright, frothy sputum, SpO₂ 82 % on a non-rebreather, BP 210/120, HR 118, crackles to the apices. She is alert and frightened.

Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary oedema: high afterload drives fluid into the lungs. CPAP or BiPAP lowers preload and afterload and recruits flooded alveoli, while high-dose nitrates lower afterload. Intubation can often be avoided.
